title: AC Conductance in n-InSb Structures with Quantum Well. Acoustic Studies
authors: I. L. Drichko, I. Yu. Smirnov, Yu. M. Galperin, A. V. Suslov
abstract: We studied the ac conductance of an $n$-InSb quantum well structure using acoustic methods in magnetic fields up to 18 T and at temperatures ranging from 20 to 500 mK. We attribute the unusual magnetic field dependences of surface acoustic wave (SAW) attenuation and velocity observed in the experiment to the presence of a conducting layer parallel to the quantum well in the sample. We successfully separated the contributions from both the quantum well and the shunting layer, enabling the identification of their distinct conduction mechanisms. Furthermore, by employing the coincidence technique, we determined the electron g-factor in the quantum well and investigated its dependence on the degree of spin polarization.
summary: This experimental work uses Surface Acoustic Waves in a high-field magnet setup to study the AC conductance of an InSb quantum well. The key innovation is successfully separating the electrical response originating from the QW itself versus that from a parallel conducting layer. This allowed for detailed characterization, including determining the electron g-factor and confirming different conduction regimes like hopping transport.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the AC conductance of an n-InSb quantum well structure while simultaneously separating its contribution from a parallel conducting shunting layer.
main_result: The authors successfully separated the conduction mechanisms, determined the electron g-factor in the QW using acoustic measurements under tilted magnetic fields, and confirmed hopping transport in both the QW and the shunting layer at high fields.
method: Acoustic methods utilizing Surface Acoustic Waves (SAW) generated on $	ext{LiNbO}_3$ are employed to measure changes in SAW attenuation ($\Delta\Gamma$) and velocity ($\Delta v/v$), which are then used to derive the complex AC conductance components.
model_or_system: The physical system is an n-InSb quantum well structure grown on GaAs, featuring a 21 nm QW shunted by a parallel conducting layer. Measurements are conducted in high magnetic fields (up to 18 T) and cryogenic temperatures (20–500 mK).
key_observables: SAW attenuation change ($\Delta\Gamma$), relative velocity shift ($\Delta v/v$), complex AC conductance components ($\sigma_{ac}$), electron g-factor ($g$).
important_parameters: Magnetic field $B$ (up to 18 T), Temperature $T$ (20–500 mK), Quantum Well width (21 nm).
main_assumptions: The ability to model and subtract the background contribution from the parallel conducting layer ($\Delta\Gamma_b(B) \propto 1/B^2$) is crucial for isolating the QW response.
figures_summary: Figures show magnetic field dependences of $\Delta\Gamma$ and $\Delta v/v$, illustrating the subtraction process to isolate QW contributions, and presenting results confirming distinct conduction regimes (e.g., hopping vs. delocalized).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes SAW measurements to derive AC conductance components ($\sigma_{QW}, \sigma_{layer}$), uses background subtraction techniques to separate the two material contributions, and finally applies a coincidence technique in tilted fields to measure fundamental parameters like the g-factor.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state transport, the use of high magnetic fields and quantum confinement effects touches upon topics relevant to strongly correlated electron systems and mesoscopic physics, which share theoretical overlap with open quantum system dynamics.
